claims.text: High configurational entropy stabilizes the mixed-metal lattice of high-entropy multi-metal nanoparticles.
Competing enthalpic contributions, including differences in atomic radii and bonding energies, can drive phase segregation under thermal stress.
The balance between configurational entropy and enthalpic contributions governs retention of a single-phase solid solution over 473–1923 K.
The initial nanoparticles are homogeneous solid solutions containing five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
Atomic-size mismatch and differences in bonding energies induce lattice strain.
Lattice strain modulates the relative importance of configurational entropy and enthalpic destabilization.
At elevated temperatures, configurational entropy stabilizes the mixed-metal lattice.
When enthalpic factors become dominant during thermal cycling, lattice strain increases.
Increased lattice strain drives localized segregation or phase separation.
Under inert or reducing conditions, the nanoparticles will largely retain a single-phase solid solution up to temperatures near 1923 K.
Minor oxidative effects or additional thermal stress that promotes enthalpic destabilization will cause phase segregation, grain-boundary diffusion, or formation of secondary phases.
External oxygen can accelerate segregation through mechanisms extrinsic to the proposed intrinsic thermal process.
Temperature ramp rates can introduce non-equilibrium effects that alter the prediction.
The threshold at which enthalpic contributions overcome entropy stabilization varies with metal combination, compositional deviation, and processing history.
XRD peak broadening can indicate lattice strain in these nanoparticles.

contradictions.description: The intervention and prediction include a mildly oxidative comparison, but the stated validity conditions and boundary restrict the hypothesis to environments in which oxidizing or other reactive species are minimized or absent. It is therefore unclear whether the oxidative arm is inside the hypothesis's scope or merely an external control.

The core hypothesis says that an entropy–enthalpy balance governs stability, whereas the primary falsification rule treats similar behavior under inert and oxidative atmospheres as falsifying. Similar behavior across atmospheres would not by itself exclude an intrinsic entropy–enthalpy balance, so the proposed result does not logically contradict the core mechanism.
